newsitem.title: FRANCE: OECD says inflation targets best EMU policy guide.
newsitem.headline: OECD says inflation targets best EMU policy guide.

text.p: Unpredictable changes in financial markets and possible innovation in financial services mean that a direct inflation target would be a more reliable guide for interest rate policy in a single European currency than monetary aggregates, the OECD said in its June Economic Outlook.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development said that if international demand for a new single currency, or euro, proved to be erratic, monetary aggregates would be volatile and may not reflect accurately the state of the European economy.
"To the extent that this proves to be the case, there will be advantages in focusing directly on inflation rather than targeting monetary aggregates," the OECD said in the report.
The report was due to be made public next Wednesday but an OECD spokeswoman said on Thursday the publication embargo had been lifted after a news agency issued details.

A recent report by the European Monetary Institute narrowed the list of potential monetary policy strategies to targeting monetary aggregates or inflation directly, or basing the policy of a future European central bank on a combination of the two.

"Volatility is the key word: as long as changes in the external demand for currencies are gradual or their size small relative to the total domestic demand for the currency, the adoption of monetary targeting in the EMU area should not destabilise macroeconomic management," the OECD said.
The German Bundesbank currently targets broad money supply growth while central banks in countries such as France and Britain use inflation targets.
The report said the impact on exchange rates of changes in currency reserve holdings at European central banks after the introduction of the euro would probably be limited.

It said the ECB's holdings would be mainly in dollars but if it wanted to diversify it could make gradual changes over time and would not be under any obligation to reduce reserves once a single currency were launched.
"Indeed it may be sensible to hold more reserves initially until the euro is firmly established," the OECD said in its report.

The OECD said the introduction of the euro could lead to "greater bilateral exchange rate volatility against the dollar and the yen than European countries have experienced in the past" and it could have a large impact on small economies whose currency is pegged to one of the major units.

It said because the European Union, the United States and Japan have limited trade exposure to each other, European monetary authorities may put less weight in the inflation impact of exchange rate movements than individual European central banks do now.

However, it said as long as the three major economic blocs pursued stable economic policies and the ECB established its credentials as a credible central bank "bilateral exchange rates among the three major economies could be more stable than they have been since generalised floating began in the early 1970s".

The OECD also emphasised that the discipline of a so-called stability and growth pact, agreed at a Dublin summit last year and due to be ratified in Amsterdam next week, was important for allowing member states to respond to economic shocks but further structural reform of labour markets was necessary.

"There is a risk of additional increases in structural unemployment and other imbalances if, in the absence of further and more fundamental structural reforms, European labour and product markets remain insufficiently flexible to respond smoothly to large asymmetric shocks," the OECD said.
The OECD also said the introduction of a single currency would reinforce restructuring of European financial services and small European derivatives exchanges would be the losers.

"While the demand for stock index contracts may continue, the need for interest rate contracts in a number of currencies will vanish...with possible negative effects on the position of smaller exchanges of countries which, in the past, have profited mainly from contracts denominated in their own currency," the report said.

It said it was too early to say which European financial centre would come to the fore in a euro zone as several key policy decisions on payment systems and reserve requirements had yet to be resolved, but there was a chance business would move away from countries not in the euro.
"With zero or low interest-bearing reserve requirements, business could eventually shift back from offshore markets to the domestic euro market," the report said.
-- David Clarke, Paris newsroom +331 4221 5452
